title: Special vote
summary: A special vote is no different to a normal vote, except special voters must also sign a declaration form when they vote.
answer:
A special vote is no different to a normal vote, except special voters must also sign a declaration form when they vote. There are several reasons why someone might need to cast a special vote. This includes if their name is not on the printed roll at a voting place by the time voting begins, this might occur because of the following reasons:

- They enrolled after the roll was printed (writ day **4 October**)
- They're voting away from your home electorate
- They're on the unpublished roll

If one of these situations apply to a voter, once they get to a voting place, they'll need to fill out and sign a 'special declaration vote' form before they can vote, then they cast their vote as normal. 

Special votes are counted in the days following the election day. Special votes also include overseas votes, [[takeaway-vote]]s, and postal votes.

title: Takeaway vote
summary: A takeaway vote is for those who cannot physically make it to a voting place during the advance voting period or on election day.
answer:
A takeaway vote is for those who cannot physically make it to a voting place during the advance voting period or on election day. For those who cannot make it to a voting place nearby, they can authorise someone else to pick up their voting papers and bring the papers to them.

Closer to the election, voters will be able to download a form from the Electoral Commission's website which they must sign to authorise someone else, they can then ask that person to take it to a voting place. The authorised person can then bring back their voting papers to complete.

If someone is unable to download and print the form, they can write the following information by hand on a piece of paper and have someone take it to a voting place. The handwritten authorisation must include:

- The voter's first and last name
- The voter's contact phone number
- The address where the voter is enrolled to vote
- The electoral roll (general or Māori) the voter believes they are enrolled on
- A statement authorising the bearer to collect voting papers on the voter's behalf.

If someone is completing a takeaway vote, their voting papers must be returned to a voting place **before** voting closes at **7pm** on election day on **7 November**.

title: Election day vote
summary: The 7th of November is the official date of the 2026 general election. It is considered the formal voting date of the general election, votes cast on this date will be counted as a regular vote (subject to some special vote exceptions).
answer:
The 7th of November is the official date of the 2026 general election. It is considered the formal voting date of the general election, votes cast on this date will be counted as a regular vote (subject to some special vote exceptions). 

On election day voting places must be open from 9am-7pm across New Zealand.

The voting places available to voters will be posted by the Electoral Commission 3 weeks before election day. 

<https://map.vote.nz/voting-places> - Closer to the voting period this link will have information for voters to check which voting place is near them.  

When someone goes to vote they can take their EasyVote card (voters should receive this in the mail or via email). If they don't have a card or forget it, they can still vote as normal.

When voters arrive to vote, someone will be there to guide them and answer any questions. 

Voters can give their EasyVote card to the person issuing voting papers or confirm their name and address to them. They’ll find the voter's name on the electoral roll and give them a voting paper. 

Once someone gets their voting paper, they will be able to take it to a voting screen where they can vote privately.

title: Advance voting
summary: Advance voting begins 12 days before election day. This means in the 2026 election, any vote cast from the 26th of October until the 6th of November is an advance vote, and any vote made on the 7th of November is counted as an election day vote.
answer:
Advance voting begins **12 days before** election day. This means in the 2026 election, any vote cast from the **26th of October** until the **6th of November** is an advance vote, and any vote made on the **7th of November** is counted as an [[election-day-vote]]. 

The process of advance voting is the same as an [[election-day-vote]], it just allows those who may be busy on election day or those who want to get in as early as possible, to cast their vote. 

There will be several advance voting places available to voters in their electorate. Voters will be able to check where all the nearby voting places are and their hours on the Electoral Commission's website 3 weeks before election day.

<https://map.vote.nz/voting-places> - Closer to the voting period this link will have information for voters to check which voting place is near them. 

When someone goes to vote they can take their EasyVote card (voters should receive this in the mail or via email). If they don't have a card or forget it, they can still vote as normal.

When voters arrive to vote, someone will be there to guide them and answer any questions. 

Voters can give their EasyVote card to the person issuing voting papers or confirm their name and address to them. They’ll find the voter's name on the electoral roll and give them a voting paper. 

Once someone gets their voting paper, they will be able to take it to a voting screen where they can vote privately.

title: Māori roll
summary: The Māori Electoral Option is a choice for all those with Māori descent on which electoral roll to choose when voting.
answer:
The Māori Electoral Option is a choice for all those of Māori descent on which electoral roll to choose when voting. 

Māori are able to choose to enrol on the Māori roll or the general roll, they can change this any time except 3 months before an election. 

This year the closing date to change rolls was **Midnight 6 August**, but if someone is Māori and still hasn't enrolled, they can still choose a roll once they complete their enrolment, the last day to complete their enrolment is **25 October**.

A voter's roll choice affects which candidates they can choose to vote for in parliamentary elections **AND** local elections for their electorate vote in particular. 

If a voter chooses the Māori roll, they will vote for a candidate in the Māori electorate they live in. If they choose the general roll, they will vote for a candidate in the general electorate they live in. 

The options when voting for a political party remains the same across both rolls. 

The roll choice is important as it helps determine the number of Māori and general electorates - the number of Māori who are enrolled on the Māori roll could mean an increase in the number of electorates, a decrease, or it can stay the same for future elections. There are currently seven Māori electorates and 65 general electorates. 

In the future, if a voter wishes to change their roll choice, they can do so easily online if they have a **New Zealand passport** or **New Zealand drivers license** or a **Realme verified login**. They can also update their roll choice by completing a paper form.

title: What is my address?
summary: Your address for the purpose of enrolment is the place you have most recently resided in for 1 month or longer.
answer:
A voter's address for the purpose of enrolment is the place they have most recently resided in for 1 month or longer.

For those who may have unstable housing conditions, who frequently move, or are overseas, they may change their **postal** address to ensure they receive any correspondence from the Electoral Commission - but their **residential** address should remain the place they last resided in New Zealand for 1 month or longer.

If someone has recently moved, but by the election date they will have lived in their current address for 1 month or longer, they may change their address to this in advance of the election date.

It is important for va voter's address to be up to date, if it isn't, they may eventually be removed from the electoral roll. The Electoral Commission will attempt to text or email voters before this happens.

title: Dormant roll
summary: If the Electoral commission is unable to reach you via email, address, or phone,  you’ll be placed on the dormant roll. When you're on the dormant roll, you're still eligible to vote but won't appear on the printed roll at voting places.
answer:
If the Electoral Commission is unable to reach a voter via email, address, or phone, they'll be placed on the dormant roll. 

When someone is on the dormant roll, they're still eligible to vote but won't appear on the printed roll at voting places. 

This means they'll have to make a [[special-vote]]. If their new address is in a different electorate to their old address, it may also mean that only their party vote will count. 

Being on the dormant roll does not affect your roll type (general or Māori). 

Once someone has been on the dormant roll for **3 years**, they will be **removed** from the electoral roll. The Electoral Commission is required to do this under the Electoral Act 1993. 

To come off the dormant roll they just need to update their address details – but they can't do this right before voting starts. To make sure they're removed from the dormant roll for the 2026 General Election, voters can check and update their details before midnight, **Sunday 25 October 2026**. 

The only other circumstances where voters are removed from the electoral roll would be if they have passed away, if they have moved overseas, or if they have become ineligible for another reason such as being sentenced to a prison term.

title: Unpublished roll
summary: If you're concerned about your personal safety, or that of your family, you can apply to go on the confidential unpublished roll. The Electoral Commission will keep your enrolment details secure and we won't give them to anyone.
answer:
If a voter is concerned about their personal safety, or that of their family, they can apply to go on the confidential unpublished roll. 

The Electoral Commission will keep a voter's enrolment details secure and they won't give them to anyone. 

Going on the unpublished roll means a voter's details won’t be included on printed electoral rolls. It also means they won't be able to check or update their enrolment details online. 

They'll need to make a [[special-vote]] at parliamentary and local elections. 

They'll need to provide information that shows why they need to register on the unpublished roll. Here are some examples of the type of information to include (they don't need all of these types of information to apply):

- A letter explaining why their work or personal circumstances place them at risk. This letter could be from their employer, lawyer, social worker, advocate, or someone of standing in the community. 
- A copy of a protection order that is in force under the Family Violence Act 2018. 
- A copy of a restraining order that is in force under the Harassment Act 1997. 
- Information from a police officer or corrections officer explaining why publishing the voter's name and address could prejudice them or their family’s safety.
